questions.subject: ComputerScience
questions.situation: A robot can't remember its own name
questions.prompt: Which of these is a VALID Python variable name?
questions.explanation: A name can't start with a digit, can't contain '-', and can't be a keyword like 'for'.
questions.hint: Rules: letters, digits and _ only, no digit first, no keywords.

questions.subject: ComputerScience
questions.prompt: Pair each built-in function with what it does.
questions.explanation: print shows, input reads, len counts, int converts.
questions.hint: Read the function names as English words.

questions.subject: ComputerScience
questions.prompt: What does the terminal print?
questions.explanation: x = x + 3 takes the OLD value of x (5), adds 3, and stores 8 back in x.
questions.hint: The right side is worked out first, then stored.

questions.subject: ComputerScience
questions.prompt: The glitch swapped two registers. What prints?

data.code:
a, b = 4, 7
a, b = b, a
print(a, b)
data.outcome: Python swaps both values at once: a = 7, b = 4

questions.explanation: a, b = b, a evaluates the right side (7, 4) first, then assigns both together, so it swaps.
questions.hint: Work out the whole right side before assigning.

questions.subject: ComputerScience
questions.prompt: How many times does the robot laugh?
questions.explanation: range(3) produces 0, 1 and 2: three values, so three HAs.
questions.hint: range(n) gives n values starting at 0.

questions.subject: ComputerScience
questions.prompt: This loop should print 1 to 5 and then STOP. Tap the bug.
questions.explanation: i goes DOWN (1, 0, -1 ...), so i <= 5 stays true forever: an infinite loop. It must be i = i + 1.
questions.hint: Which way does i move each time the loop runs?

questions.subject: ComputerScience
questions.situation: A lift that skips the top floor
questions.prompt: BUG MONSTER uses OFF-BY-ONE! This loop must print 1 to 5. Drag the correct range into the gap.
questions.explanation: range stops BEFORE the end value, so range(1, 6) gives 1, 2, 3, 4, 5.
questions.hint: range(start, stop) never includes stop.

questions.subject: ComputerScience
questions.situation: A power meter that lost its count
questions.prompt: Rebuild the program so it prints the sum of 1 to 10. Arrange the blocks.
questions.explanation: Start the total at 0, add every n inside the loop, and print once AFTER the loop finishes.
questions.hint: Indented lines belong inside the loop.

questions.subject: ComputerScience
questions.prompt: How many times does count go up?

data.code:
count = 0
for i in range(2, 20, 3):
    count += 1
print(count)

questions.explanation: range(2, 20, 3) gives 2, 5, 8, 11, 14, 17: six values.
questions.hint: List the values: start at 2, jump by 3, stop before 20.

questions.subject: ComputerScience
questions.prompt: Make the robot stop when its battery reaches 0. Fill the gap.
questions.explanation: The loop should keep going WHILE there is charge left: battery > 0. 'True' would never stop.
questions.hint: A while loop runs as long as its condition is True.

questions.subject: ComputerScience
questions.prompt: How many stars does this nested loop print?
questions.explanation: The inner loop runs fully (2 times) for each of the 3 outer runs: 3 x 2 = 6.
questions.hint: Multiply the counts of nested loops.

questions.subject: ComputerScience
questions.prompt: What do we call a loop whose condition NEVER becomes False?
questions.explanation: An infinite loop never stops because its condition never becomes False, like Lord Infinite Loop himself.
questions.hint: Think of the Lord's name.

questions.subject: ComputerScience
questions.prompt: FINAL TEST: Rebuild the GLITCH-counter. Multiples of 15 print GLITCH, multiples of 3 print GLI, others print the number.
questions.explanation: Check the most specific condition (15) first. If % 3 came first, 15 would print GLI and never GLITCH.
questions.hint: Order matters in if / elif: the first true branch wins.

questions.subject: ComputerScience
questions.prompt: What value of x leaks out of the loop?

data.code:
x = 1
for i in range(5):
    x = x * 2
print(x)

questions.explanation: x doubles five times: 1 -> 2 -> 4 -> 8 -> 16 -> 32.
questions.hint: Track x after each turn of the loop.

questions.subject: ComputerScience
questions.situation: A launch countdown that never starts
questions.prompt: This countdown should print 5, 4, 3, 2, 1. Nothing prints! Tap the bug.
questions.explanation: range(5, 0) counts UP from 5 and stops before 0, which is immediately empty. Counting down needs a step of -1.
questions.hint: Which direction does range count by default?

questions.subject: ComputerScience
questions.prompt: The lift loop runs while floor < 4, starting at floor 1 and going up 1 each time. Which floors does it visit inside the loop?
questions.explanation: It runs for 1, 2 and 3. When floor becomes 4 the condition 4 < 4 is False and the loop stops.
questions.hint: Test the condition each time BEFORE the body runs.

questions.subject: ComputerScience
questions.prompt: The weather tower reads 35. What does it display?

data.outcome: 35 > 30 is True, so only HOT prints

questions.explanation: 35 > 30 is True, so the if-branch runs and the else-branch is skipped.
questions.hint: Only one branch of if/else ever runs.

questions.subject: ComputerScience
questions.prompt: The exam gate won't compile. Tap the broken line.
questions.explanation: Every if statement must end with a colon ':'.
questions.hint: Look at the end of each line that opens a block.

questions.subject: ComputerScience
questions.prompt: x = 15. Which output appears?
questions.explanation: 15 > 10 is the first TRUE test, so B prints and the rest of the chain is skipped, even though 15 > 5 is also true.
questions.hint: In an if/elif chain, only the FIRST true branch runs.

questions.subject: ComputerScience
questions.situation: A calendar that lost a day
questions.prompt: Fix the calendar terminal: it should say 'Leap year' correctly.
questions.explanation: Leap years divide by 4, except century years, which must also divide by 400 (2000 yes, 1900 no).
questions.hint: Remember the century rule.

questions.subject: ComputerScience
questions.prompt: Repair the AND gate's truth table. Tap the ? cells to set 0 or 1.
questions.explanation: AND is 1 only when BOTH inputs are 1.
questions.hint: Both, or nothing.

questions.subject: ComputerScience
questions.situation: A door that argues with itself
questions.prompt: What does the door controller evaluate?
questions.explanation: True and False = False; not False = True; True or False = True.
questions.hint: Brackets first, then not, then and, then or.

questions.subject: ComputerScience
questions.prompt: Build the lock rule: the vault opens only when KEYCARD is present AND the ALARM is NOT on. Place the blocks in order.
questions.explanation: KEYCARD AND NOT ALARM: true only if the card is there and the alarm is off.
questions.hint: NOT goes right before the thing it flips.

questions.subject: ComputerScience
questions.prompt: Repair the XOR gate. XOR outputs 1 when the inputs are DIFFERENT.
questions.explanation: XOR is exclusive OR: 1 when exactly one input is 1.
questions.hint: Same inputs give 0, different inputs give 1.

questions.subject: ComputerScience
questions.prompt: The door code is binary 1011. Type it in decimal.
questions.hint: Add the place values that have a 1.

questions.subject: ComputerScience
questions.prompt: Write decimal 25 in binary (type only 0s and 1s).
questions.explanation: 25 = 16 + 8 + 1, so the bits are 1 1 0 0 1.
questions.hint: Take the biggest place value that fits, then repeat.

questions.subject: ComputerScience
questions.prompt: Pair each unit of data with its size.
questions.explanation: bit < nibble (4 bits) < byte (8 bits) < kilobyte (1024 bytes).
questions.hint: A nibble is half a byte.

questions.subject: ComputerScience
questions.prompt: Set the bits so the register holds 13. Drag 0 or 1 into each slot.
questions.hint: Which place values add up to 13?

questions.subject: ComputerScience
questions.prompt: Put the steps of 'find the largest number in a list' in order.

items: If this item > max, set max = this item

questions.explanation: Start with a guess, compare every item once, update when something bigger appears, output at the end.
questions.hint: You need a starting value before you can compare.

questions.subject: ComputerScience
questions.prompt: Binary search halves a sorted list each step. What is the SMALLEST number of halvings that shrinks 1000 items down to 1?
questions.explanation: Each halving divides by 2. 2^10 = 1024 >= 1000, so 10 halvings are enough, and 9 (512) are not.
questions.hint: Find the smallest power of 2 that is at least 1000.

questions.subject: ComputerScience
questions.prompt: The sorting bot runs. What is printed?
questions.explanation: sort() arranges ascending: [1, 2, 5, 9]. Index 0 is the smallest: 1.
questions.hint: Index 0 is the first item AFTER sorting.

questions.subject: ComputerScience
questions.prompt: Linear search checks names one by one. In a list of 50 names, how many checks in the WORST case?
questions.explanation: Worst case: the name is last (or missing), so all 50 are checked.
questions.hint: What if the name is at the very end?

questions.subject: ComputerScience
questions.prompt: Pair each value with its Python data type.
questions.explanation: Whole number int, decimal float, text in quotes str, True/False bool.
questions.hint: Quotes always mean text.

questions.subject: ComputerScience
questions.prompt: What does the list terminal print?
questions.explanation: Index 1 is the SECOND item (20) and index -1 is the LAST item (40). 20 + 40 = 60.
questions.hint: Indexes start at 0; -1 counts from the end.

questions.subject: ComputerScience
questions.prompt: The birthday bot crashes with a TypeError. Tap the bug.
questions.explanation: input() always returns text (str). Text + number is a TypeError, so convert with int(age) first.
questions.hint: What type does input() give back?

questions.subject: ComputerScience
questions.prompt: Which password would survive the Glitch's guessing attack longest?
questions.explanation: Long passwords mixing upper/lower case, digits and symbols are hardest to guess. Names, dates and keyboard patterns are easy.
questions.hint: Length + variety = strength.

questions.subject: ComputerScience
questions.prompt: Pair each cyber-term with its meaning.

right: a fake message that tricks you into giving data
scrambles data so only key-holders can read it

questions.explanation: Phishing tricks people, malware harms systems, firewalls filter, encryption scrambles.
questions.hint: Phishing sounds like fishing: it uses bait.

questions.subject: ComputerScience
questions.prompt: An email says: 'Your account is locked! Click here and type your password.' What kind of attack is this?
questions.explanation: Phishing: a fake message pretending to be trustworthy, to steal passwords or data.
questions.hint: It uses bait.
